question: Following the adoption of the rules on the EU guidelines for the development of the Trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T), amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1153 and Regulation (EU) No 913/2010 and repealing Regulation (EU) No 1315/2013 (TEN-T), serious concerns have been raised about the inclusion of the project to link Messina and Villa San Giovanni.

Taking account of EU legislation and the TEN-T criteria, the information available suggests that the project has not yet fully demonstrated its financial viability nor reached a sufficient stage of development. Serious unresolved environmental issues also persist.

In 2021, in its response to priority question for written answer P-001529/20211, the Commission stated that the Italian authorities had not submitted any concrete plans regarding this connection, preventing it from being able to assess the project.

The huge financial commitment foreseen for it – some EUR 15 billion – could limit the availability of resources for other projects and undermine the development and cohesion objectives by diverting key resources from other funds such as the FSC and ERDF OPs. In view of the above: 1.
Could the Commission provide an update on the project’s current stage of development, feasibility assessments and environmental impact analyses, submitted by Italy?
What is the official EU position on supporting this project with EU funds, given the serious shortcomings highlighted?
If it were to fund it, could this have a negative impact on the amount of funding available and on development and cohesion objectives?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2024) In 2023, Italy informed the Commission that studies in preparation of the project are ongoing, including the assessment under Article 6 of Directive 92/43/EEC1 and Cost Benefit Analysis.

Member States must ensure that projects likely to have significant effects on the environment are made subject to an Environmental Impact Assessment in accordance with Directive 2011/92/EU2 before authorisation. The project promoter must study reasonable alternatives relevant to the project.

The Commission is not aware of a final decision for the bridge yet, hence the maps of the revised TEN-T Regulation3 show the project as ‘study/idea’. Under the Connecting Europe Facility4, the Commission can co-fund studies aiming to prepare construction of TEN-T infrastructure projects with 50% of their total eligible costs. Only the railway part of the Messina bridge would be eligible for EU co-funding5.

Under the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF)6, regulatory thematic concentration requirements, focusing on Policy Objectives (PO) 1 ‘smarter Europe’ and 2 ‘greener Europe’, limit the allocation for large mobility infrastructures. Those are only eligible under PO3 ‘more connected Europe’.

Moreover, the Italian Partnership Agreement identifies sustainable mobility investments in rail infrastructure as priority and limits investments in road infrastructure to the selective upgrade of secondary roads connecting inner areas. Neither the Sicily nor the Calabria ERDF regional programme foresee investments in large infrastructures such as the bridge.

Without the results of the preparatory studies no assumptions can be made on a potential EU contribution to the construction activities of the planned bridge and thus on potential impacts on the overall budget.
